meta.panelHeading: Step by Step numbers in a group of 100 women
meta.tableCaption: Women at each stage of the protection order process

steps.of: Women, all eligible for a protection order
steps.head: Every one of these women could have applied
steps.body: The women interviewed were aged 18 to 45 and living in Tshwane, eThekwini, the Waterberg and the Cape Winelands. All had been beaten, strangled, raped, threatened with a weapon or stalked by a partner in the past year, so all of them qualified for a protection order. Each dot stands for about 97 women.

steps.of: Tried to apply for a protection order
steps.head: 77 Never tried
steps.body: Only 22,5% (2 181 of the 9 674) ever tried to apply. The researchers note this share may not hold for the country as a whole, but it points one way: most women who could benefit from a protection order never start the process.

steps.head: 2 Never completed the form
steps.body: Some were talked out of it by police members or court officials. Others were handed forms with no help to fill them in — and the forms must be completed in English. Some took the papers home, where their partner found them and tore them up.

steps.of: Women had a protection order granted, valid for 8 weeks
steps.head: 2 Women were not granted the order
steps.body: Nine out of ten women who applied (89,8%) were granted an interim order. The sticking point came next: an order does not take effect until the man has been informed of it. Some could not be found, some had left the area, and some were in custody, where officials sometimes wrongly said they could not be served.

steps.of: Women continued with the process to finalise the protection order
steps.head: 7 Women decided no to finalise their protection order
steps.body: Two out of every three women with an interim order applied to finalise it. Among those who did not, the most common reason was that he or his family begged her not to go through with it, promising he would change. Just as many feared that finalising it would make the violence worse. The other seven were not left unprotected: their interim order still stood for its eight weeks.

steps.of: was granted a finalised protection order, with no expiry date
steps.head: 1 Woman was not granted a finalised protection order
steps.body: When women did apply to finalise, 92,3% were granted a final order. Of the 100 we started with, 11 arrive here (1 083 women out of 9 674). But the count of women the system reached is 19: every one of them held an order that the law could enforce, whether or not it was ever made final.
